newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin heart surgery "success", but needs time.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin heart surgery "success", but needs time.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin came through seven hours of open heart surgery on Tuesday but it will be some time before Russians will know if the 65-year-old president can return to full health and stamp his authority on the Kremlin.
"The operation was a complete success," said Michael DeBakey, 88, the pioneering U.S. surgeon who acted as observer.
"President Yeltsin will be able to return to his office and carry out his duties in normal fashion," he told reporters.
But Renat Akchurin, the Russian cardiologist who led the surgical team, voiced a note of caution. "Now the very important stage of post-operative treatment is starting," he said.
He revealed the bypass surgery was more extensive than the media had been led to expect -- something Western specialists said could indicate serious problems to come.
But Akchurin said Yeltsin should be fit enough in a day or two to take back power from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Just before entering the theatre at dawn, he had handed over authority, including Russia's nuclear trigger, to Chernomyrdin, one of several figures jostling for position around him.

Doctors have said Yeltsin may need a couple of months to get fully back to work. Akchurin said it may be nearly a week before doctors could estimate how quickly and fully he would recover. But if all goes well he could leave hospital in 10 days or so.
Yeltsin's wife Naina told ORT television she was desperate to see her husband but hoped he would recover "with God's help".
The president has plenty to do.
He must calm Kremlin squabbles that have raged in his four-month absence and address the economic crisis that sparked scattered strikes and protests on Tuesday over unpaid wages.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, who faces reelection on Tuesday, sent Yeltsin "best wishes for a speedy recovery".
Western leaders see Yeltsin, who led Russia out of communism in 1991, as the best guarantor of Russia's shaky democracy and fear that, without him, Russia would become deeply unstable.
Financial markets welcomed the news the long-awaited surgery had gone ahead smoothly. Russian stock and bond prices rose.

The 50-year-old Akchurin, grey with fatigue after a dawn start and confiding he had tried to forget he was operating on the president, said Yeltsin might not come round before midnight (2100 GMT). Medical staff could then take him off a respirator.
Indicating the president's heart trouble was more grave than admitted, he said the number of blockages in his arteries was "much more" than the three or four forecast.
He said the details were Yeltsin's "personal business" and what mattered was that his heart was getting plenty of blood.

But independent specialists said the added complexity of the surgery might mean more problems. Professor Michael Rees of Bristol Royal Infirmary in England said: "It could lead to prolonged recuperation or complications in the future."
A Western cardiologist in Moscow said the multiple bypasses raised a risk of further heart attacks and suggested Yeltsin might have been better off with a wholesale heart transplant.
The president faces the biggest risks after the surgery. Two German specialists in post-operative complications are on hand.
But the sense of relief was already palpable at the clinic.

"The operation went better than I expected," said Yevgeny Chazov, the head of Moscow's Cardiology Research Centre where the operation was carried out. Chazov kept increasingly senile Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev alive for a decade in the 1970s.
Yeltsin, who opted for surgery rather than a passive wait for death, issued a statement before the operation saying he was confident and reassuring Russians there was no power vacuum.
"Not for a minute will the country be without a leader with full powers," Yeltsin said. "He (Chernomyrdin) and my other colleagues are tested and reliable people."
Chernomyrdin, 58, and a possible successor, has effectively been running the country since Yeltsin's reelection on July 3.
The president had announced the operation on television in a moment of unprecedented candour on September 5. It ended weeks of equivocation by aides who had said he simply had a cold.
The admission that the president, after two heart attacks last year, needed major surgery also fuelled a bitter struggle for influence in the Kremlin.
It involved notably Chernomyrdin, chief of the presidential staff Anatoly Chubais and General Alexander Lebed, a political maverick roped in to the Kremlin to secure victory at the polls.

Yeltsin finally sacked Lebed on October 17 amid a flurry of accusations and counter-accusations of mysterious plots and plans to seize power. Lebed has warned of an army mutiny over unpaid wages, but few analysts see a military bid for power.
If Yeltsin died, Chernomyrdin would rule for three months pending fresh elections.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, 52, would also be a challenger in a new vote. He complained the Kremlin cheated to beat him in July by concealing that Yeltsin had had a third heart attack days before the second-round vote.
